reasons_add: Mawardi describes light breaking over the eastern horizon, distinguishes the vanishing upright false dawn from the horizontally spreading true dawn, and cites a poet calling the latter truthful. Alusi derives the name from splitting the night and also glosses it as dawn's column or spreading light. Ibn Ashur describes the first eastern solar ray pushing back darkness before sunrise.

Tabari holds that the oath denotes morning dawn; Mawardi reports Ali's daily morning view. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan call daily dawn the majority view; Ibn Kathir adds Ali, Mujahid and al-Suddi among its proponents. Durr says al-Hakim authenticated Ibn Abbas's general-daybreak report. Alusi prefers true dawn because prayer and fasting attach to it. Ibn Ashur says the generic article best fits the coordinated night in 89:4 and reports Qatada identifying the daily dawn-prayer time.

Ibn Kathir also attributes this view to Masruq and Muhammad ibn Kab, as the close of the ten nights. Qurtubi's Ibn Abbas report says this day has no night before or after and that a pilgrim reaching the standing place after Arafah still catches the pilgrimage until this dawn. Biqai calls it the complete dawn, magnified as though no other dawn existed. Ibn Ashur says its article would indicate a previously known day and locates the pilgrims at Muzdalifa. Durr's Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Kab reports expressly exclude every dawn.

Baghawi specifies Atiyya's transmission from Ibn Abbas. Razi argues that the prayer gathers night and day angels and that 17:78 describes its recitation as witnessed. Ibn Kathir also attributes the prayer reading to Ikrima. Alusi allows either an omitted noun or figuratively naming the prayer itself.

Razi associates the first day with recurring observances and lunar reckoning and reports Ibn Abbas calling Muharram the year's dawn. Qurtubi specifies a chain through Atiyya and Ibn Muhaysin for Ibn Abbas's report. Alusi identifies Said ibn Mansur and Bayhaqi's al-Shuab as transmitters of the Ibn Abbas report.
Mawardi and Qurtubi explain naming the entire daytime by its beginning. Razi compares the oaths by forenoon and by day as it becomes clear (93:1; 92:2).
Baghawi and Qurtubi transmit al-Dahhak's inference from the adjacent ten nights (89:2); Razi says this dawn opens the month of the great pilgrimage rite.
Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan specify springs breaking from rocks, while Razi says their gushing water sustains living creatures.

Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Alusi attribute the Muzdalifa view to Muqatil. Qurtubi reports Ikrima's day at Jam and Muhammad ibn Kab's final day of the ten when pilgrims depart; Ibn Ashur situates the Sacrifice-day dawn while pilgrims are at Muzdalifa.
Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Alusi attribute Friday dawn to Ikrima.

Mawardi describes false dawn as an upright, narrow column that vanishes, leaving darkness before morning, and calls it misleading or the herald of morning; true dawn spreads horizontally and truthfully announces morning. Alusi says this legal distinction makes true dawn likelier as the oath's referent.
Tabari and Durr transmit Ibn al-Zubayr's statement that God swears by dawn; Qurtubi counts five oaths in the opening passage.
Alusi permits supplying an omitted noun for the dawn prayer, alongside a figurative construal naming the prayer itself.
Durr transmits Maymun ibn Mihran's contrast between God's freedom to swear by any creation and the human restriction to swearing by God.

Abu Hayyan reports Abu al-Dinar's tanwin on al-fajr, al-watr and yasr; Ibn Khalawayh and an unnamed poet illustrate rhyme-ending tanwin even on verbs and definite forms. Abu Hayyan compares unrestricted rhyme without tarannum, two prose stopping patterns, and treatment of verse endings as rhymes.

Razi says oath objects have religious benefit as signs of oneness, worldly benefit calling for thanks, or both; their perceived priority drives interpretations. He links dawn to 74:34, 81:18 and God as maker of daybreak (6:96). Ibn Ashur calls the first light a display of divine power and artistry; it releases people from death-like sleep into aware, useful work. He says the times sworn by display God's craftsmanship and include times of worship.

Razi compares creatures emerging at dawn with the dead rising from graves and calls it a lesson for reflection. Biqai says night and day renewing after disappearance demonstrate the power to resurrect. Ibn Ashur compares the end of sleep with a return from death.

Razi explains the Day of Sacrifice's offering as a substitute for self-sacrifice the worshipper cannot make, citing 37:107. Biqai evokes return to the Sacred House, release from consecration and divine hospitality, and describes this dawn as complete and singularly grand.
Ibn Ashur says an oath calls God to witness an assertion; God's own oaths serve to confirm that assertion.

Ibn Ashur connects dawn's transition from darkness with the fully dark night and says generic dawn best suits its coordination with night in 89:4; the other sworn times are also associated with worship.
Baghawi and Qurtubi report al-Dahhak arguing from the neighboring ten-night oath (89:2); Razi adds that the first dawn opens the month of pilgrimage.

Abu Hayyan relates the earlier warning against turning away and disbelief to the later warning that God lies in wait (citing 92:16 and 89:14). Biqai reads pilgrimage clothing, talbiya and journey to appointed places as reminders of return and resurrection. Alusi transmits Suyuti's comparison between the openings' questions, including 88:17.

Abu Hayyan connects al-Ghashiya's downcast and radiant faces (88:2, 88:8) with the deniers and tranquil soul (89:27); Alusi also follows that contrast. Ibn Ashur says the sura warns Meccan polytheists through Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, promises the Prophet his enemies' decline, and refutes treating prosperity as divine honor and believers' poverty as humiliation; failure to share and greed lead to regret over neglecting faith and good works.

Ibn Atiyya calls the Meccan view more famous and sounder. Durr transmits Meccan attributions from Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and Aisha. Nasafi gives 29 verses; Alusi and Ibn Ashur specify 32 in Medina and Mecca, 30 in Kufa and Syria, and 29 in Basra. Ibn Ashur places revelation tenth after al-Layl and before al-Duha and identifies differing boundaries at niamahu, rizqahu, bi-jahannam and fi ibadi.

Ibn Atiyya reports Abu Amr al-Dani's citation of some scholars for Medinan revelation but judges Meccan sounder; Abu Hayyan and Alusi name Ali ibn Abi Talha for the Medinan view. Ibn Ashur treats the Meccan classification as agreed apart from that report.
Ibn Kathir and Durr transmit Jabir's account of the Prophet rebuking Muadh for lengthening prayer and suggesting al-Fajr among shorter suras, alongside al-Ala, al-Shams and al-Layl.

Durr reports Muharram as the best voluntary fasting month after Ramadan, with night prayer best after obligatory prayer; another report recalls a day of repentance and forgiveness. Ashura reports recount Moses' rescue, the Prophet's order to fast, Ansar families helping children fast with wool toys, and Ibn Abbas's special esteem for its fast. Al-Aswad says only Ali and Abu Musa among Kufan Companions urged it. Reports propose fasting the ninth, the day before or after, or both adjacent days to differ from Jews. Ibn Shihab fasted it while traveling because its opportunity cannot be made up; Abu Musa mentions the Jewish festival and Abu Hurayra the prophets' practice.

Durr supplies reports through Jabir, Ibn Masud, Abu Said and Abu Hurayra, as well as Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn al-Muntashir's reported saying. Al-Bayhaqi regards the separate weak chains as mutually strengthening.
Durr transmits the promise through Ibn Abbas and notes Bayhaqi's judgment that it is weak.

question: 89:1/q15
position: Muharram is called God's greatest month.
reasons: Razi relays an unnamed report using this description without supplying a chain or grading.

question: How is the sura titled in transmitted texts?

positions.position: Surat al-Fajr, without the opening oath waw.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur says Quran copies, commentaries and hadith books consistently use this title.

question: Can al-fajr and the neighboring oath terms have more than one referent?

positions.position: Shared terms can denote multiple things, with either one or several senses intended.
positions.reasons: Al-Suyuti lists dawn, the ten nights, even and odd among examples of terms whose referents can be multiple; whether both senses are intended varies.

question: 89:1/q10
position: The extended oath sequence builds anticipation for its eventual assertion.
reasons: Ibn Ashur says the accumulated oaths make the listener await the statement they confirm.

question: Whom does the opening oath address?

positions.position: The Prophet directly, while indirectly assuring deniers that the assertion will occur.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur infers the address to the Prophet from the later reminders of God's acts against Ad and of divine watchfulness (89:6, 89:14).
